  "passage_locator": {
    "label": "GHOST STORIES. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER VI. / LEGENDS.; lines 15703-15807",
    "start": "15703",
    "end": "15807",
    "translation": "Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "The passage strings together several demonic legends and editorial comparisons: a demon who stole a peasant's crust becomes his helpful hireling, a soldier protects a princess from nightly fiends and traps them in a knapsack marked with a cross, and a sorcerous peasant visits the devils' realm to find a bride for his son and learns of the fiery 'Gossip's Bedstead' before fleeing.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Satan orders that the peasant's stolen crust be restored.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "The demon who stole the crust turns himself into a good youth and becomes the peasant's hireling.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "The hireling scatters seed over a swamp before drought and sows hill slopes before a wet season, so the peasant fills his barns while others lose their crops.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "An evil spirit comes every night at midnight to a princess's chamber and troubles her until dawn.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "A soldier lights the room, stops the fiend after it takes the form of a man, plays cards with it, tricks it, and beats it with a 'three-man beetle.'",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4", "ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "Satan sends further devils night after night for a month, then comes himself and is beaten back to his swamp.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "The soldier gets the fiends into his knapsack, signs it with a cross so they cannot get out, and has it thumped on an anvil.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "When women open the knapsack in the soldier's absence, the fiends rush out and fling themselves into the pool below a mill-wheel.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "A poor peasant learns sorcery, becomes acquainted with devils, and goes to their realm to seek a bride for his grown son.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "The devils offer a girl who drank herself to death and who carries water for them.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:11",
      "text": "At the wedding feast, Satan offers a receipt from a father who sold his son, but a devil has hidden it and will not reveal where it is.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:11"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:12",
      "text": "The hidden receipt is surrendered when Satan orders the devil to be stretched on the Gossip's Bedstead, which Satan describes as fiery, wheeled, and turning round and round; the peasant then flees in fear.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:11", "ev:12"]
    }
  ],
  "figures": [
    {
      "id": "fig:1",

heroic.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A crowd of warriors rushes forward so quickly that they mistake the gray, dun, and foods.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The youth fastens the string of scalps to a long pole, raises it over his shoulder so the lower scalps will not drag, and cedars.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the fire is extinguished, Tó`nenili, the Navaho, and Hastsézini leave in single file, dwelling and names color-coded sacred cigarettes by which the spell can be removed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The narrative explains that such cigarettes are into the hollow log, plug it again, and set it floating down the river.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"When the log sticks at a fall in the San Juan River, the sloping.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The man's pet turkey is heard gobbling four times, approaches from the east, circles him sunwise at south, west, and stature.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that the story of the Volsungs and Niblungs has entered the literature of GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9087-9190","start":"9087","end":"9190","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes summarize ceremonial corn symbolism, requirements for sacred corn, the category of nátli, hunting masks, the quarrel and separation of First Man and First Woman, the rise of anáye, directional waters and birds, the sky-reaching reed during rising waters, digging animals reaching the upper waters, and Locust's ordeals.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Yellow corn is assigned to the female and white corn to the male, and this rule is said to be observed in Navaho ceremonies and mentioned in many myths.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"An ear of corn used for sacred purposes must be fully grained, and in some rites it must be tipped by four grains; such an ear is called tohonoti'ni.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The note explains nátli or nu'tle as anomalous persons or as men who dress as women and perform women's work, and says they are credited in the legend with inventing arts practiced by women.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Masks made from deer-head or antelope-head skins are described as hunting devices used to deceive animals, and the note says Navaho tales and rites mention them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"First Woman thanks her vagina after eating; First Man objects, they argue over the dependence of women and men, and he jumps across the fire in anger.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"During the separation of the sexes, both men and women commit shameful practices, and the women's transgressions bring the anáye into existence.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The four waters are color-coded by direction: east black, south blue, west yellow, and north white; a ritual picture is said to represent Tiéholtsodi and the four waters.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A great reed is said to have grown to the sky; one version says spider wove the nodes and animals lived in different internodes, while another says the reed grew by day and rested by night.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Turkey is said to have been the last to enter the reed and to have stayed at the bottom, warning the others when the rising waters came close.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Bear, Wolf, Coyote, Lynx, and Badger dig upward until water from the upper world begins to drip down, after which Locust is sent up and makes a shaft in the mud.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Versions describe four directional birds and an ordeal involving arrows or an axe, and they explain Locust's narrow face and large chest by these events.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10","ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"First Man","description":"Male primordial figure who quarrels with First Woman and jumps across the fire.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"First Woman","description":"Female primordial figure who thanks her vagina after text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A sequence of editorial notes discusses Navaho food taboos, a fish-related purification incident, an old hunting method, place-name and gens-name explanations, a winter moccasin game with an associated day/night animal contest myth, poor clothing and borrowed arts in earlier times, use of fibrous tissue and cave storehouses, and an alternate mountain-route naming tradition.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that modern Navahoes do not eat ducks, snakes, or fish, and that fish are feared.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A white woman poured fish-soaked water over a young Navaho man, who then changed clothes and bathed to purify himself.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"An old method of hunting deer and antelope involved driving them onto a high mesa with a narrow connection and forcing them over a precipice.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The name To`-do-kón-zi is explained from a word for water and a term translated as saline or pleasantly salty.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The old arrow-case is known only by tradition and is said to have resembled a modern shawl-strap.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A tree described in the notes is said still to stand and is identified in the note as apparently a large birch.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Kesitsé is a winter night game played inside a lodge, with eight buried moccasins arranged in two rows on either side of a fire.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In the game, a black-marked chip determines which side begins, one side hides a stone in a moccasin behind a screen, and the opposing side guesses its location and exchanges counters based on success.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The game is associated with a myth of a contest between animals who hunt by day and animals who hunt by night.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Before sheep and weaving, the Navahoes are described as poorly clothed, and weaving is said to have probably been learned from Pueblo peoples.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Useful arts are said to have become known to the tribe through adopted members of other tribes.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Small caves and rock-shelters were walled up and used as store-houses rather than dwellings.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Another version explains the name Base of Mountain through a woman who urged travelers to remain along the base of the Lukachokai Mountains.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The final note cautions that one statement should be qualified because it     "label": "III. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9369-9472",
    "start": "9369",
    "end": "9472",
    "translation": "Navaho Legends",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "This note cluster describes several sacred mountains and landmarks in Navaho tradition, their directional colors and associated materials, several named boy/girl pairs linked to corn, pollen, goods, and jewels, the Place of Emergence in the northern mountains, a mirage-stone kept by ritual specialists, and a ritual mixture of waters from multiple sources and directions.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "Do-kos-líd / San Francisco Mountain is described as the sacred western mountain, with yellow and yellow objects belonging to the west, and haliotis shell treated as sacred to it.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "White Corn Boy and Yellow Corn Girl are glossed from white or yellow corn plus boy or girl, and the note says there may be more than one divine pair with these names.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Depe'ntsa / the San Juan Mountains are said to bound the land on the north; the Place of Emergence lies among them, and black things belong to these mountains.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Pollen Boy and Grasshopper Girl are named again, and Grasshopper Girl is depicted in corn pollen in a dry-painting.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },

GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9963-10063","start":"9963","end":"10063","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Explanatory notes describe life-feathers and pollen, a Spider Woman episode in which two brothers are hardened through obsidian and turquoise, their journey through supernatural barriers to the house of the Sun, the colored sentinels at the entrance, and their reception of special armor and weapons.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A life-feather or breath-feather is a feather taken from a live bird, especially a live eagle; it is believed to preserve life, possess magic powers, and be used in rites.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Pueblo Indians are said to rear captured eaglets for such feathers, while Navahoes are said to trap full-grown eagles and pluck them while alive.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Pollen is described as an emblem of peace.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In Spider Woman's house there are four ladder rungs; the elder brother sits on obsidian, the younger on turquoise; she offers four kinds of food and they accept one kind.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"An obsidian image comes from an eastern apartment, the elder brother stands beside it on a serrated platform, and Spider Woman blows four times so that he acquires the hard nature of obsidian.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A turquoise image comes from the south room, the younger brother stands beside it on a serrated platform, and Spider Woman blows toward it so that he acquires the hard nature of the blue stone.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"On the way to the house of the Sun, the brothers are threatened by Tiéholtsodi the water monster and appease it with prayer; Old Age People receive them kindly and warn them away from the trail to the house of Old Age.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Daylight rises like a great range of mountains and lets the brothers pass under; Wind gives them songs for Darkness, which also rises and lets them pass under; they then walk over water.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After crossing the water, the brothers meet their sister, the daughter of the Sun, and follow her silently to the Sun's house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"At the entrance to the house there are groups of four sentinels behind curtains; in each group the colors are black, blue, yellow, and white, and the brothers sing to them and sprinkle pollen on them.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"When they enter the house, the brothers are said to come seeking their father.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Each brother receives four articles of armor and six kinds of weapons, including lightning arrows, sunbeam arrows, rainbow arrows, a stone knife-club, and a thunderbolt or great stone knife.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The note explains that the word for the armor originally referred to flint knives or flakes, and it reports the author's conclusion that the mythic armor was conceived as stone-flake armor rather than iron.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Black Thunder and Blue Thunder are named as two young men, and once equipped the brothers are dressed exactly like them.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"elder brother","description":"One of the two brothers; he sits on obsidian, stands beside the armed.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:6","ev:7","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Spider Woman","description":"A female figure in whose house the brothers are EXCERPTS FROM THE POETIC EDDA / SELECTED BIBLIOGRAPHY: / RECOMMENDED READING-- / INTRODUCTION; lines 409-493","start":"409","end":"493","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage presents a Norse cosmological overview: the gods order the world from Ymir's remains, create Midgard and the first humans Ask and Embla, describe Asgard and several gods, recount Loki's monstrous children and the burning and renewal of the world, describe Yggdrasil and its springs, the Norns and creatures of the tree, Valhall and its daily cycle, and a venomous hall for murderers and oath-breakers.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The gods make clouds from Ymir's brain and set sparks from Muspellheim in the sky as lights.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The earth is round, the deep sea lies around it, the giant kind receive the outer shore, and Midgard is made as a burg from Ymir's brows against giants.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The gods find two stocks and shape from them a man and a woman, giving soul, life, wit, movement, face, hearing, speech, sight, clothing, and names.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The first humans are named Ask and Embla, and mankind is given an abode under Midgard.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Asgard is a burg in the midst of the world where the gods dwell; Odin sits in a high seat seeing the whole world, and Frigg is his wife.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Earth is called daughter and wife of Odin, and Thor is begotten of her.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Thor possesses Miolnir, a strength-belt, and iron gloves; Balidr, Tyr, and Bragi are praised for fairness, courage, wisdom, speech, and song.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Loki is fair-faced but ill-tempered, slanderous, and crafty.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Fenris-wolf and Midgards-worm are among Loki's children; the worm lies round the world in the sea and Fenris is bound until the gods' doom.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"At the doom of the gods Fenris slays Odin, earth and heaven burn, and afterward the earth rises green from the sea and gods and men are alive again.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Yggdrasil's ash spreads over the world and above heaven; its roots reach heaven, the region of the Hrimthursar and Mimir's spring, and Niflheim where Nidhogg gnaws.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Norns shape the lives of men; an eagle, hawk, squirrel, and worm inhabit the ash, and the Norns sprinkle the tree with water and clay to keep it from withering.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The battle-slain come to Valhall, where a boar is renewed daily, a she-goat gives mead, Odin is attended by wolves and ravens, the heroes fight by day and feast afterward, and a venomous hall stands for murderers and oath-breakers.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:10","ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"the gods","description":"They order the sky and earth, make Midgard, shape     "summary": "Sun-father instructs two brothers how to recover all parts of their dead mother so she can live again, warns them against killing certain game, transforms and dresses them in his likeness, and is recognized as their father. He sends them back to their Badger foster parents, who do not at first know them. The boys then recount that their mother came from the Home of the Eagles, was killed by the Twain during an escape on an Eagle, and that the Badgers reared them after their birth.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]

      "id": "obs:2",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },

      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Sun-father says the boys have power to slay game, but forbids them to kill rabbit, deer, antelope, mountain sheep, or elk, warning that they would perish with their mother.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]

    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Sun-father removes bark moccasins and dresses the younger brother, then the elder, in fine leggings, buskins, garters, a quiver, and plumes.",

      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3", "ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "Sun-father creates a warm cloud of mist that cleanses the boys so their skin becomes smooth and clear and their hair falls in wavy masses.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "After seeing their resemblance to him and recalling their mother's appearance, the boys recognize the Sun as their father.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "Sun-father says he must return to his home in the heavens and tells the boys to go back to the Badgers carrying their bark moccasins, strings of corn-cakes, and the rabbits they have slain.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "Sun-father passes his hands over the dead rabbits, making them light enough to carry, and then is no longer visible after the boys depart.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "At the Badgers' home, the foster mother does not recognize the transformed boys until they show their bark moccasins and strings of corn-cakes.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7", "ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "The boys say their mother once lived at the Home of the Eagles and was killed by the Twain while escaping on the back of an Eagle.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:11",
      "text": "The boys say they were born when their mother fell into the Cañon of the Coyote, and the Badgers found and reared them.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:12",
      "text": "Badger-father says there will be a dance at the Home of the Eagles in eight days and that the boys will go there when the day comes.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]

He abducts a king’s daughter after taking the form of a bull, later turns her into a heifer, fathers Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto, divides heaven, earth, and hell among them, and is eventually overthrown by Jupiter. After fleeing to Italy under the name Njord, he teaches agriculture and builds settlements there.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Saturn grows up in Crete, surpasses other men in strength, beauty, and wisdom, invents crafts, practices magic, and foretells future events.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Saturn discovers a red substance in the earth from which he smelts gold, becomes powerful, is chosen chief of the island, and prosperity follows in Crete.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Because of Saturn’s power and secret gifts, men believe him to be God, and Saturn calls himself God and ruler of heaven and earth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Saturn goes to Greece by ship, takes the likeness of a bull in a wood, wins a king’s daughter, carries her to the ship, and brings her to Crete.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After Juno finds out, Saturn turns the king’s daughter into a heifer, sends her east to the Nile country, places Argulos over her, and restores her shape after twelve months.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Saturn has three sons—Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto. Thor.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Saturn builds seventy-two burgs in Crete and distributes realms to his sons: heaven to Jupiter, earth to Neptune, and VII. / ON THE WONDERFUL THINGS IN HEAVEN. / CHAPTER VIII. / THE ASAS.; lines 1972-2040","start":"1972","end":"2040","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage catalogs several asas and their attributes: Brage and Idun with youth-restoring apples, Heimdal as vigilant guardian near Bifrost with the Gjallarhorn, Hoder, Vidar, Vale, and Uller with notable traits, and Forsete in Glitner reconciling disputes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Brage is described as famous for wisdom, eloquence, and flowing speech, and as a master-skald.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Song-craft is called brag from Brage, and eloquent men and women are called brag-men and brag-women.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Idun is Brage's wife and keeps apples in a box; when the gods grow old they eat them and become young again, and this continues until Ragnarok.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ganglere says Idun's keeping of the apples must be important to the gods, and Har says the gods once ran a great risk concerning them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Heimdal is also called the white-asa, Hallinskide, and Gullintanne; he is said to be born of nine maidens who were sisters, to have gold teeth, to ride the horse Gulltop, and to dwell at Himinbjorg near Bifrost.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Heimdal is the ward of the gods and sits at the end of heaven guarding the bridge against the mountain-giants.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Heimdal needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred miles by night and day, and hears the grass grow and the wool on sheep.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Heimdal has a trumpet called the Gjallarhorn, and when he blows it it is heard in all the worlds; the head is called Heimdal's sword.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Hoder is blind and exceedingly strong, and the gods would wish that he never needed to be named because the work of his hand will long be remembered.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Vidar is called the silent asa, has a very thick shoe, is strongest next after Thor, and gives the gods much help in hard tasks.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Vale is the son of Odin and Rind, daring in combat, and a good shot.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Uller is the son of Sif and stepson of Thor; he is an excellent archer, very fast on skees, fair of face, and men should invoke him in single combat.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Forsete is the son of Balder and Nanna, Nep's daughter, and has in heaven the hall called Glitner; all who come to him with disputes go away perfectly reconciled.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Glitner is described as standing on gold pillars and being roofed with silver.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"A footnote compares brag with Anglo-Saxon brego, glossed as princeps or chief.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Brage","description":"An asa famous for wisdom, eloquence, flowing speech, and poetic Har names several dwellings and their inhabitants or features, including Alfheim, Breidablik, Glitner, Himinbjorg, Valaskjalf with Odin's high-seat Hlidskjalf, and Gimle, a bright hall that will remain after heaven and earth pass away for the good and righteous. now.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ganglere asks whether there are other remarkable places than the one by Urd's dwell.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The dark-elves are said to dwell down in the earth and to differ from the light-elves in appearance and markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes Frost as a personified natural power who freezes waters and cools a red-hot bath, then summarizes several related Russian tale variants: a stepdaughter abandoned in the forest who serves a supernatural Head and is rewarded, a contrasting disobedient stepdaughter who is destroyed, an ovin encounter where cockcrow determines whether a girl escapes with gifts or is torn apart, and a Vikhor tale in which a whirlwind abductor carries off a queen and her sons begin a search.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Frost is described as a mighty smith who forges chains to bind the earth and the waters.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A proverb describes a frozen river as a bridge built without axe or knife.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Moroz-Treskun enters a bath heated red-hot for a hero and turns its heat to cold with icy breath.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage states that the Frost story is known in many lands and has many Russian variants.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In one tale a woman orders her husband to get rid of his daughter by a previous marriage.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The husband leaves the girl in a forest hut and deceives her by tying a log to a tree so that it rattles in the wind.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A human head answers the girl, is lifted over the threshold, eats with her, and sleeps in the hut.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"While the girl sleeps, the head goes into the forest, and the house becomes larger and fills with servants and horses.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The girl rides with the head, brings a cock, and after the cock crows three times the head breaks apart into golden coins.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The stepmother's daughter refuses to help the head and is eaten.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In another tale a stepdaughter watching rye in an ovin is asked to marry a stranger, who brings wedding items one by one until cockcrow makes him disappear.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The stepsister asks for all of the items at once, finishes dressing before cockcrow, and the stranger tears her to pieces.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The passage says that in Russian tales the abductor may be called Vikhor instead of Koshchei or the Snake.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In the Vikhor tale a gale carries off a queen, and her three sons ask to seek her after learning that Vikhor took her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Frost / Moroz-Treskun","description":"A personified Frost described as a smith who binds earth and waters and as a being whose icy breath cools a red-hot bath.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Certain woman / stepmother","description":"A woman her in a hut, and deceives her with a rattling log.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Human Head","description":"A human head in the forest that answers the girl, dines with her, later appears with servants and horses, and falls to pieces into golden coins after cockcrow.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Stepmother's daughter","description":"The stepmother's own daughter, who refuses to help the head and is eaten.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Stranger in the ovin tale","description":"A stranger who appears by night in the ovin, asks a girl to marry him, sent to watch rye in an ovin who requests wedding clothes one item at a time and leaves with gifts after cockcrow.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Stepsister in the ovin tale","description":"The second girl in the ovin tale, who asks for all items at once YOUTH AND HIS EAGLE                                 34 / A HOPI (MOKI) MAIDEN                                   184 / THE PINNACLES OF THUNDER MOUNTAIN                      344 / INTRODUCTION; lines 290-378","start":"290","end":"378","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory expository passage defines widespread Amerindian concepts of magical power under the borrowed term “orenda,” illustrates ritual transfer of power from serpent to arrow and conflict between opposed powers, links song and worship to magical efficacy, describes shamans and origin myths, and outlines a regional cosmology centered on a midworld with upper, lower, and cardinal worlds.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage says Amerindian languages have terms for magical power, including Iroquoian orenda, Siouan wakan or wakanda and hube, and Shoshonean pokunt.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Unexplained phenomena are attributed to orenda.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Serpent venom is described as orenda that can be conveyed to an arrow by ritual action, including invocation, placing a rattlesnake beside the arrow, or dipping the arrow in a serpent brew.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In an Iroquois example, one ancient planned the streams of earth by his orenda, but his wicked brother interfered and changed the arrangement, showing one orenda thwarting another.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Birdsong and human singing are both described as exercises of orenda, and song is said to accompany worship universally.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Diseases and ailments are attributed to orenda, and tales are said to teach some method by which death and disease entered the world through supernatural agencies.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Shamans are described as prophets, priests, wonder-workers, and medicine-men; they may be initiated by guild ceremony or revelation, and failed practitioners may be treated as witches.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Origin myths are said to explain striking phenomena such as animal features, including the buffalo’s horn, the rabbit’s shoulder patch, and the snake’s rattle.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The cosmology described includes a central world, an upper world, a lower world, and four cardinal worlds.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Animals, bodies of water, mountains, rocks, and even colors are said to have proper habitation in these regions and to come to the midworld from them.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The passage compares this regional cosmology to a three-part heaven-earth-hell model used in the
